entry: Metropolitan and ceremonial county in North West England (pop., 2024: 3,009,664). Its largest settlement is the city of [[Manchester]], at the center of a county that covers 1,276 sq km and is highly urbanized. It was created in 1974 from parts of north-east [[Cheshire]], south-east [[Lancashire]], and the West Riding of Yorkshire. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], its towns became major centers for the manufacture of [[Cotton|cotton]] textiles. After deindustrialization in the mid-20th century, the county became a center for service, media, and digital industries. It is also recognized for its contributions to guitar and dance music and for its football teams.

Series of armed conflicts between Greek city-states and the [[Achaemenid Empire]] from 499 BC to 449 BC. Also called the Persian Wars, they grew out of Persian rule over Ionia, which [[Cyrus the Great]] conquered in 547 BC. The Ionian Revolt of 499 BC, incited by Aristagoras of Miletus, prompted the Persian king [[Darius the Great]] to punish Athens and Eretria, which had helped capture Sardis. A Persian force was defeated at the [[Battle of Marathon]] in 490 BC. In 480 BC [[Xerxes I]] invaded with a large army, winning the [[Battle of Thermopylae]] and razing Athens. The Persian fleet was defeated at Salamis that year, and the Persian army at Plataea in 479 BC. The Greek [[Delian League]] then campaigned against Persian forces in Asia Minor and Cyprus. The conflicts ended around 449 BC, and some ancient sources say the purported Peace of Callias formally resolved them.

Country in southeastern Europe on the Balkan peninsula, officially the Hellenic Republic. Its capital, [[Athens]], is the largest city, and the population is around 10 million. With up to 227 inhabited islands, the country has the longest coastline on the Mediterranean basin. The region was home to the [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greek]] city-states, which are regarded as the birthplace of democracy, historiography, political science, and the [[Olympic Games]]. [[Philip II of Macedon]] united most of the area in the 4th century BC. Most Greek lands came under Ottoman control by the mid-15th century, and a war of independence that began in 1821 led to a modern nation state in 1830. A transition to democracy began in 1974, leading to a parliamentary republic. Greece joined the [[European Union]] in 1981 and has a developed, high-income economy in which shipping and tourism are major sectors.

Insatiable desire for material or social gain, often at the expense of others. Also called avarice, greed may target food, money, land, possessions, status, or power. Modern economic thought frequently distinguishes greed from self-interest. In Classical Greek thought, [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] discussed an unjust desire to gain at others' expense. [[Christianity]] counts avarice among the [[Seven deadly sins]], and the Sanskrit *Dharmashastras* call greed the root of all immorality. Late-Republican and Imperial writers, including [[Cicero]] and [[Plutarch]], blamed greed for wealth and power for the fall of the [[Roman Republic]]. As a psychological concept, greed is an inordinate desire to acquire more than one needs, and it has been found to relate to financial behavior, unethical behavior, and lower well-being.

Successful revolt by Greek revolutionaries against the [[Ottoman Empire]], fought from 1821 to 1829. Greek lands, except the Ionian Islands, had been under Ottoman rule since the decades surrounding the [[Fall of Constantinople]]. The secret Filiki Eteria had planned an uprising for March 25, 1821, but its discovery forced an earlier start. The Maniots declared war on March 17, and Greek forces captured Tripolitsa in September 1821. Civil wars among the Greek factions led the Ottoman sultan to call in [[Muhammad Ali of Egypt]], whose son Ibrahim Pasha brought most of the Peloponnese under Egyptian control by the end of 1825. [[British Empire|Britain]], France, and the [[Russian Empire]] intervened in 1827, destroying the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino. Greece was recognized as independent under the London Protocol of February 1830, and Prince Otto of Bavaria became its first king. The revolution's slogan, "Freedom or death", became the national motto.

Script used to write the [[Greek language]] since the late 9th or early 8th century BC. It was derived from the earlier [[Phoenician alphabet]] and is the earliest known alphabetic script to write [[Vowel|vowels]] systematically as well as [[Consonant|consonants]]. The Ionic-based Euclidean alphabet of 24 letters, ordered from alpha to omega, became standard by the end of the 4th century BC and is still used for Greek writing. Throughout antiquity Greek had only one uppercase form of each letter, and Byzantine scribes had begun using lowercase forms by the 9th century. The alphabet is the ancestor of the [[Latin script]], the [[Cyrillic script]], and other scripts, and its letters serve as international symbols in mathematics, science, and other fields. Ancient and Modern Greek use different sound values and diacritics.

Incendiary weapon used by the [[Byzantine Empire]] from the 7th to the 14th centuries. Its recipe was a closely guarded state secret and has been lost. Most modern scholars believe it was based on [[Petroleum|petroleum]] mixed with [[Resin|resins]], comparable to [[Napalm]]. Byzantine sailors threw [[Grenade|grenades]] of it onto enemy ships or sprayed it from tubes. It could burn on water, and rival powers tried unsuccessfully to copy it.

American rock band formed in Rodeo, California, in 1987. It is credited with reigniting mainstream interest in [[Punk rock|punk rock]]. Its 1994 album *Dookie* shipped over 20 million copies in the United States. The rock opera *American Idiot* (2004) sold six million copies in the US, and a stage adaptation debuted on Broadway in 2010. The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2015 and has won five [[Grammy Awards|Grammys]]. It has sold roughly 75 million records worldwide.

Agricultural movement in which technology transfer significantly increased crop yields. It emerged in developed countries in the early 20th century and spread globally until the late 1980s. Its high-yielding varieties of [[Wheat|wheat]] and [[Rice|rice]] required chemical [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], [[Pesticide|pesticides]], and controlled [[Irrigation|irrigation]]. The term was first used by William S. Gaud of the U.S. Agency for International Development in a speech on March 8, 1968. The Ford and Rockefeller foundations were heavily involved in its initial development in Mexico. [[Norman Borlaug]], known as the Father of the Green Revolution, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 and is credited with saving over a billion people from starvation. Yuan Longping's work on hybrid rice is credited with saving at least as many lives. Studies show that the movement contributed to the widespread eradication of poverty, averted hunger for millions, and declines in infant mortality.

Paraphyletic group of chlorophyll-containing autotrophic algae. Green algae range from unicellular and colonial [[Flagellate|flagellates]] to coccoid and filamentous forms, and to macroscopic seaweeds. There are about 22,000 species. Their [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] contain chlorophyll a and b, and their cell walls usually contain [[Cellulose|cellulose]]. They store carbohydrate as [[Starch|starch]]. Together with land plants, they form the clade Viridiplantae. Some green algae live symbiotically in the ciliate [[Paramecium]], and others form [[Lichen|lichens]] with fungi. Members of the class Chlorophyceae undergo [[Mitosis|closed mitosis]], while charophytes and land plants undergo open mitosis.

Unripe, young fruit of cultivars of the common bean, *Phaseolus vulgaris*. Green beans are sold fresh, canned, and frozen, and can be steamed, boiled, stir-fried, or baked. They are commonly added to [[Soup|soups]] and [[Stew|stews]]. Raw green beans are 90% water, 7% [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], and 2% [[Protein (nutrient)|protein]], with a moderate amount of [[Vitamin C]] and vitamin K. Some German sources advise against eating them raw, because they contain a lectin that high temperatures destroy. The first stringless bean was bred in 1894 by Calvin Keeney in Le Roy, New York. Green bean casserole, made with cream of mushroom soup and French-fried onions, is common at [[Thanksgiving]] in the northern U.S.

Color between cyan and yellow on the [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]]. It has 295–350 shades and is evoked by light with a dominant [[Wavelength|wavelength]] of roughly 495–570 nm. In subtractive color systems it is made by combining yellow and cyan, while in the [[RGB color model|RGB model]] it is one of three additive primaries. By far the largest contributor to green in nature is [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]], the pigment by which plants photosynthesize. The emerald is green because of its [[Chromium|chromium]] content. In post-classical and early modern Europe, green was associated with wealth and merchants, while red was reserved for the nobility. It is the traditional color of [[Ireland]] and was the color of the banner of [[Muhammad]]. In surveys in American, European, and Islamic countries, green is most associated with nature, life, health, youth, spring, hope, and envy.

Large, arboreal, mostly herbivorous [[Lizard|lizard]] of the genus *Iguana*. It is native from southern Brazil and Paraguay as far north as Mexico, and was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1758 as *Iguana iguana*. It grows to 1.7 m (5.6 ft) in length, and a few specimens have exceeded 2 m (6.6 ft), with bodyweights upward of 9 kg (20 lb). Its herbivorous diet has led to significant adaptations in locomotion and osmoregulation. The species is highly invasive in many subtropical and tropical environments, including [[Puerto Rico]] and [[Hispaniola]]. Because of its disposition and coloration, it is commonly kept as a [[Pet|pet]], although its requirements for space, lighting, and heat are difficult for hobbyists to meet.

[[Ideology|Political ideology]] focused on an ecologically sustainable society. Also called ecopolitics, it is often rooted in [[Environmentalism|environmentalism]], nonviolence, social justice, and grassroots democracy. It took shape in the Western world in the 1970s, and green parties have since won some electoral success in many countries. The term green was first used in relation to *die Grünen*, a German party formed in the late 1970s. Supporters share ideas with the conservation, environmental, [[Feminism|feminist]], and peace movements, and the ideology is concerned with [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]] and social justice. Green party platforms are largely considered left on the [[Political spectrum|political spectrum]]. Its ethical stance draws on the values of [[Indigenous peoples|indigenous peoples]] and on the ethics of [[Baruch Spinoza]].

Unoxidized [[Tea|tea]] made from the leaves and buds of *Camellia sinensis*. Unlike [[Black tea|black]] and oolong teas, its leaves do not undergo the withering and oxidation process. Green tea originated in [[China]] in the late 1st millennium BC and spread to other East Asian countries. Lower-quality green teas are steeped hotter and longer than higher-quality teas, and steeping too hot or too long releases excessive tannins. As of 2015, China provided 80% of the world's green tea market and exported 325,000 [[Tonne|tonnes]]. While green tea may slightly lower [[Blood pressure]] and improve alertness, excessive intake of green tea extracts can damage the liver, interfere with [[Prescription drug|prescription drugs]], and cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

Atmospheric heat retention by heat-trapping [[Greenhouse gas|gases]]. Greenhouse gases absorb the longwave radiation emitted by a planet's surface, so less heat escapes to space and the surface warms. Surface heating can come from an internal source, as on [[Jupiter]], or from a host star, as with the [[Sun]] for [[Earth]]. Without the effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about −18 °C, compared with a 20th-century average of about 14 °C. Burning fossil fuels has increased [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and [[Methane|methane]], and global warming of about 1.2 °C had occurred by 2023 since the [[Industrial Revolution]]. [[Joseph Fourier]] proposed the effect in 1824, and Nils Gustaf Ekholm first applied the term greenhouse to it in 1901.

Heat-trapping gas in a planet's atmosphere. The five most abundant greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere are [[Water vapor]], [[Carbon dioxide]], [[Methane]], [[Nitrous oxide]], and [[Ozone]]. Water vapor causes about half of the [[Greenhouse effect|greenhouse effect]] and acts mainly as a feedback to other gases. Since the [[Industrial Revolution]], human activities have increased carbon dioxide by over 50% and methane by 150%. Carbon dioxide causes about three-quarters of global warming, mostly from burning fossil fuels. Emissions have been at an all-time high of 53.6±5.2 Gt CO₂e per year over 2014–2023.

Autonomous territory of the Kingdom of [[Denmark]] and the world's largest island. It lies between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans, east of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, and its capital is [[Nuuk]]. Norsemen settled the southern part in the 10th century, and their descendants disappeared in the late 15th century. Greenland was transferred from Norway to Denmark in 1814. The 1953 Constitution of Denmark ended its colonial status, Denmark granted home rule in 1979, and Greenlanders voted for self-government in 2008. Denmark retains control of citizenship, monetary policy, security, and foreign affairs. Most residents are [[Inuit]], and the population of 56,583 (2022) makes Greenland the least densely populated country in the world. Its mineral wealth and strategic position make it important to Denmark, [[NATO]], and the European Union. Sixty-seven percent of its electricity comes from renewable energy, mostly [[Hydropower|hydropower]].

Body of water between [[Greenland]] and [[Svalbard]] in the Arctic. Often counted as part of the [[Arctic Ocean]] or the Atlantic, it is part of the Nordic Seas along with the [[Norwegian Sea]]. The sea has an Arctic climate, with temperatures rarely above 0 °C (32 °F). The West Ice forms in winter north of [[Iceland]] and is a major breeding ground for harp and hooded seals, which have been hunted for more than 200 years. The sea was a popular whaling ground for about 300 years, until 1911, when the whale population was too depleted to be profitable. Russian expeditions under Admiral V. Chichagov made the first scientific explorations in 1765 and 1766. [[Fridtjof Nansen]] described its complex water current system in 1909.

Second-largest body of ice in the world, covering about 80% of [[Greenland]]. The ice sheet covers 1,700,000 sq km and averages 1,673 m in thickness, reaching over 3,488 m at its maximum. A single ice sheet first covered most of the island some 2.6 million years ago, and it has both grown and contracted significantly since then. Because of [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions, it is now the warmest it has been in the past 1,000 years and is melting two to five times faster than before 1850. Snowfall has not kept up since 1996. If the entire sheet melted, global sea levels would rise by about 7.4 m (24 ft).

Large [[Shark|shark]] of the family Somniosidae, found in the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. It has the [[Longevity|longest lifespan]] of any known [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]], estimated at 272 to 510 years, and reaches sexual maturity at around 150 years of age. The largest confirmed specimen measured 6.4 m (21 ft) in length. It is a generalist feeder that eats carrion, and its flesh is toxic to mammals because of high levels of trimethylamine N-oxide. In [[Iceland]], a treated form is eaten as the fermented delicacy *kæstur hákarl*.

Alias for the UTC+00:00 [[Time zone|time zone]]. The Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, counts local mean time from midnight, and the term is the basis of civil time in the [[United Kingdom]]. Because of Earth's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] and uneven orbital speed, noon GMT is rarely the exact moment the Sun crosses the Greenwich meridian. British mariners used GMT chronometers to calculate [[Longitude|longitude]], and GMT came to be used worldwide as a standard time. English speakers often use GMT as a synonym for [[Coordinated Universal Time]], although it should not be used where precision is required.

Act of communication acknowledging another person's presence. Greetings exist in all known human cultures, and customs are highly specific to culture and situation. In Western cultures the handshake is very common, though grip and dominance vary, and facial expression and eye contact signal the type of greeting expected. Men traditionally tipped or removed their hats in greeting until the mid-20th century, and [[Louis XIV]] of France is said to have made a point of touching his hat to all women he encountered. In [[Early modern period|early modern Europe]], a man greeted an upper-class woman by holding and kissing her hand. Among Christians in [[Poland]], the phrase "Praise the Lord" was common before [[World War II]]. Written greetings in letters and emails are called salutations, and secret societies have used secret handshakes so that members could recognize each other.

Austrian biologist and Augustinian friar. Born into a German-speaking family in the Silesian part of the [[Austrian Empire]], he later became abbot of St. Thomas' Abbey in Brno. From 1856 to 1863 he cross-bred [[Pea|pea]] plants, establishing many of the rules of [[Heredity|heredity]] now called [[Mendelian inheritance]]. When a true-breeding yellow pea was crossed with a green one, all the offspring produced yellow seeds, but green reappeared in the next generation at a ratio of 1 to 3. He coined the terms dominant and recessive and published his work in 1866. Its significance was recognized only after Erich von Tschermak, Hugo de Vries, and Carl Correns independently verified his findings in 1900. He is regarded as the founder of the modern science of [[Genetics|genetics]].

Solar calendar used in most parts of the world for civil purposes. It was introduced in October 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII through the papal bull *Inter gravissimas*, as a modification of the [[Julian calendar]]. [[Leap year|Leap years]] occur in years divisible by four, except century years not divisible by 400, so the average year is 365.2425 days long. The reform advanced the date by 10 days, so Thursday, October 4, 1582 was followed by Friday, October 15, 1582, restoring the [[Equinox|March equinox]] to its date for the calculation of [[Easter]]. Protestant and [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox]] countries adopted it gradually, and Greece was the last European country to adopt it, in 1923, for civil use only. Many Orthodox churches still use the Julian calendar for religious rites.
